title: Methane glows from a six-Jupiter-mass brown dwarf
freshness: Accepted by Astronomy & Astrophysics on 24 September 2026 and posted publicly on 25 September 2026, within the preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: Webb detected two infrared emission lines from methane in a young brown dwarf weighing about six Jupiters. Methane usually leaves absorption features in cool atmospheres, so the glow points to unusual heating or radiation high above this object's visible surface.
whyItMatters: The finding exposes chemistry that current brown-dwarf atmosphere models do not yet explain and provides a new way to probe the upper layers of objects that bridge giant planets and the smallest products of star formation.
whatToExploreNext: Why a molecule produces dark absorption bands in one atmosphere but bright emission lines in another.
body:
## Methane shining instead of dimming the light

Methane is glowing in the atmosphere of a young brown dwarf. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers detected two emission lines at wavelengths of 3.324 and 3.333 micrometres from LRL 11001, an object estimated to weigh about six times as much as Jupiter. It is the first detection of 3.33-micrometre methane emission from a young brown dwarf.

Brown dwarfs form from collapsing clouds like stars, but never become massive enough to sustain ordinary hydrogen fusion. LRL 11001 belongs to IC 348, a roughly five-million-year-old star-forming cluster about 313 parsecs, or 1,020 light-years, away. Its low mass places it near the territory of giant planets, even though it formed in a stellar nursery.

Methane normally reveals itself by absorbing selected wavelengths from a warmer background. An emission line means molecules are releasing extra light instead. Something must therefore be exciting methane in a high atmospheric layer or another region associated with the brown dwarf.

## A sharper look at an unexplained spectrum

Earlier low-resolution Webb spectra had found an unexpected absorption band near 3.4 micrometres in several low-mass brown dwarfs in IC 348. Models had not predicted that feature. The new study revisited LRL 11001 with Webb's Near-Infrared Spectrograph at about ten times higher spectral resolution, covering wavelengths from 1.7 to 5.1 micrometres. Each of two instrument settings accumulated 1,500 seconds of exposure.

The sharper spectrum split what had looked like a simple peak into two partially blended emission lines. Their wavelengths match hot-band transitions of methane. The feature was present at the target's position in all three nods, separate placements along the spectrograph slit used to distinguish the source from background light.

The same spectrum clarified the neighbouring 3.4-micrometre absorption band. Four fitted components match vibrations of CH2 and CH3 groups, indicating a large alkane. The smallest molecule consistent with those groups is propane, although the data do not identify one exact chain length. Webb also recorded narrow carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide absorption that probably comes from ice in the object's surroundings or its molecular cloud.

## The source of the glow remains open

The authors consider two broad explanations for the methane emission. Heat deposited by an accretion shock could create a temperature inversion, leaving an upper layer warmer than the gas below. Alternatively, radiation from nearby cluster members or an accretion hot spot could pump methane molecules into excited states, much as sunlight drives fluorescent methane emission on Jupiter.

The team argues that the brown dwarf's atmosphere is a more likely source than a surrounding disk because these particular methane transitions have not been observed in disks around other young stars or brown dwarfs. That conclusion is not final. The existing spectrum shows no short-wavelength disk excess, but observations beyond five micrometres are still needed to check for cooler disk material. Detailed atmospheric modelling is also required to distinguish heating from fluorescence.

**Measured:** Webb resolved methane emission at 3.324 and 3.333 micrometres and an adjacent absorption pattern consistent with a large alkane.

**Inferred:** The methane probably glows in the upper atmosphere, but the energy source and the role of any disk remain uncertain.
